[1] James Watt
While working as an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow, Watt became interested in the technology of steam engines. He realised that contemporary engine designs wasted a great deal of energy by repeatedly cooling and reheating the cylinder. Watt introduced a design enhancement, the separate condenser, which avoided this waste of energy and radically improved the power, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness of steam engines. Eventually he adapted his engine to produce rotary motion, greatly broadening its use beyond pumping water.

[2] James Watt biography
James Watt was born in Greenock, Scotland, in 1736. He attended Greenock Grammar School but did not attend university. Instead, he was apprenticed to a mathematical instrument maker in London and later worked as an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow.

[3] James Watt early life
Watt's formal education ended at age 19 when his mother died and his father's business failed. He moved to London to learn the trade of instrument making under John Morgan for a year before returning to Scotland.

[4] University of Glasgow history
The University of Glasgow has employed many notable figures, including James Watt as an instrument maker from 1757 to 1764, where he met John Roebuck and began his work on steam engines.
